topic.name: Properties of Definite Integrals Involving the Limits of Integration

question.text: Suppose that $f(x)$ is a function such that ${\displaystyle \int_2^{-2}\dfrac14 f(x) \; \textrm{d}x = -3}$ and $ \displaystyle \int_2^5 f(x) \; \textrm{d}x = 10.$ What is the value of ${\displaystyle \int_{-2}^5 f(x) \; \textrm{d}x}?$
question.explanation:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

\[ \eqalign{ \int_2^{-2}\dfrac14 f(x) \; \textrm{d}x &= -3\\[5pt] \dfrac14\int_2^{-2} f(x) \; \textrm{d}x &= -3\\[5pt] -\dfrac14\int_{-2}^2 f(x) \; \textrm{d}x &= -3 \\[5pt] \int_{-2}^2 f(x) \; \textrm{d}x & =12 } \]

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

\[ \eqalign{ \int_{-2}^5 f(x) \; \textrm{d}x &= \int_{-2}^2 f(x) \; \textrm{d}x+ \int_{2}^{5} f(x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 12 + 10 \\[5pt] & = 22. \\ } \]

example.title: Evaluating a Definite Integral Using Multiple Properties of Definite Integrals

question.text: Given that $\displaystyle \int_{2}^{3}f(x)\,\textrm d x = -4$ and $\displaystyle \int_{3}^{8}f(x)\,\textrm d x =7$ then what is $\displaystyle \int_{2}^{8}\Big(5f(x)+4\Big)\,\textrm d x?$
question.explanation:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

\begin{align} \displaystyle \int_{2}^{3}f(x)\,\textrm d x + \displaystyle \int _{3}^{8}f(x)\,\textrm d x = \int_{2}^{8}f(x)\,\textrm d x. \end{align}

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

\begin{align*} (-4) + 7 = \int_{2}^{8}f(x)\,\textrm d x \\[5pt] 3 = \int_{2}^{8}f(x)\,\textrm d x \end{align*}

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

\begin{align} \int_{2}^{8}\Big(5f(x)+4\Big)\,\textrm d x &=5\int_{2}^{8}f(x)\,\textrm d x + 4\int_{2}^{8}\,\textrm d x \\[5pt] &= 5(3)+4 \cdot x \, \Big|_{2}^8 \\[5pt] &=15+4(8-2) \\[5pt] &=39. \end{align}

example.title: Evaluating a Definite Integral Given Integrals Over Adjacent Intervals

question.text: Given that ${\displaystyle \int_{1}^{-1} f(x) \, \textrm d x = -1},$ calculate ${\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1} \big(f(x) - 6x\big) \, \textrm d x }.$
question.explanation:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result: \begin{align} \int_{-1}^{1} f(x) \, \textrm d x = -\int_{1}^{-1} f(x) \, \textrm d x = 1 \end{align}

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get \begin{align*} \int_{-1}^{1} \big(f(x) - 6x\big) \, \textrm d x & = \int_{-1}^{1} f(x) \, \textrm d x - 6 \int_{-1}^{1} x \, \textrm d x \\[5pt] &= 1 - 6 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot x^2 \,\Big|_{-1}^{1} \\[5pt] & = 1 - 3(1^2 - (-1)^2) \\[5pt] & = 1 - 3 \cdot 0 \\[5pt] %& = -2 + \dfrac{27}{2} \\[5pt] &= 1. \end{align*}
